 perform flash wear leveling, block pre-erasing (`ACMD23`), and multi-plane NAND interleaving. `CMD25` allows the card to stream incoming data continuously into multi-cluster erase blocks without bus pauses. Decomposing to `CMD24` defeats the card's internal write pipeline.\n1047:     - **The Commercial Production Solution**: If our edge NAS required enterprise-grade throughput (e.g. multi-channel 4K video surveillance or high-frequency multi-user concurrent transfers), an embedded engineer would **never use 1-bit SPI mode in production**. Instead, the system would be migrated to the **ESP32's native 4-bit SDMMC hardware peripheral (`SD_MMC.h`)** using dedicated pins (GPIO 14, 15, 2, 4, 12, 13) with direct DMA transfers. This bypasses SPI bit-banging entirely and delivers **20 MB/s to 40 MB/s** sustained multi-block throughput. In simulation (Wokwi), however, 4-bit SDMMC is unsupported, making our 4 MHz VSPI with `CMD24` decomposition the optimal, production-reliable design for virtual microprocessor evaluation.\n1048: \n1049: ---\n1050: \n1051: ## 10.  perform flash wear leveling, block pre-erasing (`ACMD23`), and multi-plane NAND interleaving. `CMD25` allows the card to stream incoming data continuously into multi-cluster erase blocks without bus pauses. Decomposing to `CMD24` defeats the card's internal write pipeline.\n1047:     - **The Commercial Production Solution**: If our edge NAS required enterprise-grade throughput (e.g. multi-channel 4K video surveillance or high-frequency multi-user concurrent transfers), an embedded engineer would **never use 1-bit SPI mode in production**. Instead, the system would be migrated to the **ESP32's native 4-bit SDMMC hardware peripheral (`SD_MMC.h`)** using dedicated pins (GPIO 14, 15, 2, 4, 12, 13) with direct DMA transfers. This bypasses SPI bit-banging entirely and delivers **20 MB/s to 40 MB/s** sustained multi-block throughput. In simulation (Wokwi), however, 4-bit SDMMC is unsupported, making our 4 MHz VSPI with `CMD24` decomposition the optimal, production-reliable design for virtual microprocessor evaluation.\n1048: \n1049: ---\n1050: \n1051: ## 10. 303: ---
304: 
305: ### 4.3 Scenario 1: Home Hybrid Testing (Host on Wired Ethernet, Client Phone/Laptop on Router Wi-Fi)
306: In this home setup, your host workstation running the simulation is plugged into the Wi-Fi router via physical Ethernet cable, while your smartphone, tablet, or secondary laptop connects wirelessly to the same router:
307: 
308: ```
309:                       +------------------------------------------+
310:                       |         Home Wi-Fi Router Gateway        |
311:                       |          (Subnet: e.g. 192.168.0.1)      |
312:                       +--------------------+---------------------+
313:                                            |
314:                     +----------------------+----------------------+
315:                     | (Physical Ethernet)                         | (Wi-Fi 2.4/5 GHz)
316:                     ▼                                             ▼
317: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
318: |  Host PC (Running Simulation)         |     |  Mobile Device / Secondary Laptop     |
319: |  Ethernet IP: e.g., 192.168.0.105     |     |  Wi-Fi IP: e.g., 192.168.0.120        |
320: |  wokwigw.exe listening: 0.0.0.0:9080  |     |  Opens Browser to Host Ethernet IP:   |
321: |  setup_firewall.bat PORT 9080 ALLOWED |     |  http://192.168.0.105:9080/          |
322: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
323: ```
324: 
325: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
326: 1. **Find the Host Ethernet IP**:
327:    - On the host PC running the simulation, open PowerShell and execute:
328:      ```powershell
329:      ipconfig
330:      ```
331:    - Locate the section titled **`Ethernet adapter Ethernet`** (or `Ethernet adapter vEthernet` / your main wired NIC):
332:      ```text
333:      Ethernet adapter Ethernet:
334:         Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . :
335:         Link-local IPv6 Address . . . . . : fe80::...
336:         IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.0.105  <--- COPY THIS IP
337:         Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
338:         Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.0.1
339:      ```
340:    - Note the **`IPv4 Address`** (for example: `192.168.0.105` or `192.168.1.50`).
341:    > [!IMPORTANT]
342:    > Do **not** look for "Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi" on the host PC if it is plugged in via Ethernet! The host PC is communicating through its wired NIC, so client devices must target the host's **Ethernet IPv4 address**.
343: 
344: 2. **Verify Network Profile**:
345:    - Standard home routers bridge Ethernet LAN ports and Wi-Fi into the exact same broadcast subnet (`192.168.0.x`).
346:    - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator once to ensure inbound port 9080 is permitted.
347: 
348: 3. **Connect from Phone/Laptop**:
349:    - Ensure the phone or secondary laptop is connected to your home Wi-Fi SSID.
350:    - Open Chrome, Safari, or Firefox on the mobile device and navigate to:
351:      - **NAS File Dashboard**: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/` (e.g. `http://192.168.0.105:9080/`)
352:      - **Hosted Static Webpage**: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/site`
353:

356: ### 4.4 Scenario 2: Lab Workstation Testing (Both Devices on Wired Ethernet LAN Switch)
357: In the microprocessor laboratory, both the host workstation running the simulation (PC 1) and peer student workstations (PC 2) are connected via physical RJ45 Ethernet patch cables to the same campus lab switch:
358: 
359: ```
360:                       +------------------------------------------+
361:                       |         Campus Lab Ethernet Switch       |
362:                       |       (Local Subnet: e.g. 10.100.x.x)    |
363:                       +--------------------+---------------------+
364:                                            |
365:                     +----------------------+----------------------+
366:                     | (Ethernet Cable 1)                          | (Ethernet Cable 2)
367:                     ▼                                             ▼
368: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
369: |  Lab PC 1: Host Node (Simulation)     |     |  Lab PC 2: Peer Client Workstation    |
370: |  Ethernet IP: e.g., 10.100.22.45      |     |  Ethernet IP: e.g., 10.100.22.48      |
371: |  wokwigw.exe listening: 0.0.0.0:9080  |     |  Opens Chrome/Edge (No Install Needed)|
372: |  setup_firewall.bat PORT 9080 ALLOWED |     |  http://10.100.22.45:9080/            |
373: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
374: ```
375: 
376: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
377: 1. **Ensure Both PCs are Plugged Into the Lab Switch**:
378:    - Both PC 1 and PC 2 should have active link lights on their Ethernet ports.
379: 2. **Retrieve PC 1 Ethernet IP**:
380:    - On PC 1, open PowerShell and run:
381:      ```powershell
382:      ipconfig
383:      ```
384:    - Copy the `IPv4 Address` under `Ethernet adapter Ethernet` (e.g. `10.100.22.45` or `192.168.1.105`).
385: 3. **Run Firewall Setup on PC 1**:
386:    - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator on PC 1.
387: 4. **Access from PC 2**:
388:    - On PC 2, open any browser and enter `http://<PC1_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/`.
389:    - PC 2 can now immediately download files from the ESP32 or upload assembly programs and reports without installing any software.

394: During project defense or when network access in the lab is restricted (e.g. campus Wi-Fi has strict Client/AP Isolation blocking inter-device communication), turn your host laptop into a Wi-Fi Access Point using Windows Mobile Hotspot:
395: 
396: ```
397: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
398: |  Host Laptop (Windows 10 / 11)                                                    |
399: |  1. Enable Windows Mobile Hotspot (Share over: Wi-Fi)                             |
400: |  2. Windows automatically assigns Host Gateway IP: 192.168.137.1                  |
401: |  3. wokwigw.exe listens on 0.0.0.0:9080 (Binds directly to virtual hotspot NIC)  |
402: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
403:                                           ▲
404:                                           │ (Direct Wi-Fi 2.4/5 GHz Connection)
405: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
406: |  Evaluator / Peer Mobile Device (Smartphones, Tablets, External Laptops)          |
407: |  1. Connect to Laptop Hotspot SSID                                                |
408: |  2. Open Mobile Browser -> http://192.168.137.1:9080/                             |
409: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
410: ```
411: 
412: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
413: 1. **Enable Mobile Hotspot on Host Laptop**:
414:    - Press `Win + I` $\rightarrow$ **Network & internet** $\rightarrow$ **Mobile hotspot**.
415:    - Set **Share my internet connection from**: `Ethernet` (or `Wi-Fi` if connected to campus Wi-Fi).
416:    - Set **Share over**: `Wi-Fi`.
417:    - Toggle **Mobile hotspot** to **ON**.
418:    - Note the **Network name (SSID)** and **Password**.
419: 2. **Deterministic Gateway IP (`192.168.137.1`)**:
420:    - Windows automatically assigns the host PC the virtual IP **`192.168.137.1`** on the Microsoft Wi-Fi Direct Virtual Adapter.
421:    - This IP is **always identical** across all Windows machines, making it completely predictable for live presentations.
422: 3. **Connect Client Mobile Devices**:
423:    - On evaluators' or team members' phones/tablets, connect to the laptop hotspot SSID.
424: 4. **Browse Endpoints**:
425:    - Open any mobile browser and navigate to:
426:      - **NAS Dashboard**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/`
427:      - **Static Site**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site`
428: 5. **Why This is the Ultimate Presentation Safeguard**:
429:    - It forms a 100% self-contained private wireless LAN completely independent of campus firewalls, router port filtering, or internet outages.

48: ## 1. System & Architecture Overview
49: 
50: [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](.) contains a fully self-contained local simulation setup for an **ESP32-based Embedded Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Static Web Server**. Designed for the `CSE0611324` Microprocessor & Microcontrollers laboratory curriculum, it runs completely on your workstation without cloud dependencies or upload rate limits.
51: 
52: ```
53:                       +---------------------------------------------------+
54:                       |               Host Workstation                    |
55:                       |   VS Code + PlatformIO + Wokwi Simulator Engine   |
56:                       +-------------------------+-------------------------+
57:                                                 |
58:                                     ws://localhost:9011
59:                                                 |
60:                                                 ▼
61:                                     +-----------------------+
62:                                     |     wokwigw.exe       |
63:                                     | (Listens: 0.0.0.0:9080)|
64:                                     +-----------+-----------+
65:                                                 |
66:                          +----------------------+----------------------+
67:                          |                                             |
68:                          ▼                                             ▼
69:             [Wired Ethernet Interface]                    [Windows Mobile Hotspot]
70:              IP: e.g., 192.168.1.105                        Virtual IP: 192.168.137.1
71:                          |                                             |
72:                          ▼                                             ▼
73:             Lab Workstations / PCs                       Smartphones & Tablets
74: ```
75: 
76: ### 1.1 Embedded Hardware Architecture
77: * **Target Microcontroller**: Classic ESP32 DevKit V1 powered by the Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 microprocessor operating at 240 MHz, with 520 KB on-chip SRAM.
78: * **Storage Medium**: Hardware VSPI-driven MicroSD Card module formatted with standard FAT32 block storage.
79: * **Firmware Framework**: Native Arduino-ESP32 core (`WebServer.h`, `SD.h`, `SPI.h`, `WiFi.h`).
80: 
81: ### 1.2 Hardware VSPI & Storage Pinout
82: The storage subsystem directly interfaces with the ESP32 hardware VSPI bus via physical GPIO pins defined in [`src/main.cpp`](src/main.cpp) and [`diagram.json`](diagram.json):
83: 
84: | ESP32 Hardware Pin | Signal Function | MicroSD Module Pin | Description |
85: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
86: | **`GPIO 5`** | **`CS`** (SS) | `CS` | Chip Select (Active Low) |
87: | **`GPIO 18`** | **`SCK`** | `SCK` / `CLK` | Serial Clock |
88: | **`GPIO 23`** | **`MOSI`** | `DI` | Master Out Slave In |
89: | **`GPIO 19`** | **`MISO`** | `DO` | Master In Slave Out |
90: | **`3V3`** | **`VCC`** | `VCC` | 3.3V Regulated Power |
91: | **`GND`** | **`GND`** | `GND` | Ground Reference |
92: 
93: ### 1.3 Zero-Overhead Streaming Architecture
94: To prevent SRAM exhaustion on the 520 KB microcontroller during multi-megabyte file transfers:
95: * **Uploads**: Handled via `server.upload()` chunk-by-chunk streaming directly to the SD filesystem.
96: * **Downloads**: Handled via `server.streamFile()` in binary chunk buffers.
97: * **RAM Footprint**: Fixed at approximately **~2 KB** of heap memory regardless of whether transferring a 10 KB assembly program or a 20 MB binary image.
98: 
99: ### 1.4 Dual-Core FreeRTOS Task Separation
100: The ESP32 firmware leverages dual-core Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP):
101: * **Core 0**: Dedicated strictly to the lwIP (Lightweight IP) TCP/IP protocol stack and asynchronous Wi-Fi driver packet handling.
102: * **Core 1**: Runs the primary application event loop (`server.handleClient()`), SD card FAT32 sector reads/writes, and automated self-diagnostic health checks pinned via `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`.
103: 
104: ### 1.5 Dual-Network Gateway Routing Model
105: Virtual Wi-Fi inside the Wokwi simulator uses a private virtual subnet (`10.13.37.2`). The companion bridge binary [`wokwigw.exe`](wokwigw.exe) bridges this virtual subnet to the host:
106: * Communicates with Wokwi over WebSocket on `ws://localhost:9011`.
107: * Forwards host port `9080` to virtual ESP32 port `80` via:
108:   ```powershell
109:   .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
110:   ```
111: * Binds to `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`), making the simulator reachable over **Localhost**, **Physical Ethernet LAN**, and **Windows Mobile Hotspot Wi-Fi** at the same time.
112:

115: ## 2. Prerequisites & Extension Setup
116: 
117: ### 2.1 Required Software & Extensions
118: Ensure your workstation has the following installed:
119: 1. **Visual Studio Code** (version 1.80+ recommended).
120: 2. **PlatformIO IDE Extension** (`platformio.platformio-ide`):
121:    - Handles the GCC Xtensa compiler toolchain, Arduino-ESP32 core libraries, and binary compilation.
122: 3. **Wokwi Simulator Extension** (`wokwi.wokwi-vscode`):
123:    - Provides cycle-accurate hardware simulation and virtual SPI/Wi-Fi peripherals.
124: 
125: ### 2.2 Wokwi License Activation
126: If this is your first time using the Wokwi extension in VS Code:
127: 1. Press `F1` (or `Ctrl + Shift + P`) to open the Command Palette.
128: 2. Type and select **`Wokwi: Request License`**.
129: 3. Follow the one-time browser verification link to claim your license.
130: 
131: ### 2.3 Opening the Workspace Correctly
132: > [!IMPORTANT]
133: > To prevent path mismatch errors, open the directory [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](.) directly in VS Code (`File` > `Open Folder...`).
134: >
135: > If you open the top-level repository root (`Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab`), you must tell Wokwi where to find the configuration:
136: > 1. Press `F1` $\rightarrow$ select **`Wokwi: Select Config File`**.
137: > 2. Pick [`wokwi.toml`](wokwi.toml).
138:

141: ## 3. Step-by-Step Simulation Execution
142: 
143: Follow these steps in exact order to launch the simulation successfully:
144: 
145: ```
146: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
147: |  Step 0: Automated Environment & Dependencies (setup/install_dependencies.bat)     |
148: |                                     ▼                                             |
149: |  Step 1: Compile Firmware (PlatformIO Build: Ctrl + Alt + B or build_firmware.bat)|
150: |                                     ▼                                             |
151: |  Step 2: Configure Windows Firewall (Run setup_firewall.bat as Admin)              |
152: |                                     ▼                                             |
153: |  Step 3: Launch Gateway (.\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80 or .bat)      |
154: |                                     ▼                                             |
155: |  Step 4: Launch Wokwi Simulation (diagram.json -> Wokwi: Start Simulator)         |
156: |                                     ▼                                             |
157: |  Step 5: Verify Serial Output & Access http://localhost:9080/                      |
158: +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
159: ```
160: 
161: ### Step 0: Automated Environment & Dependency Setup (setup/)
162: The [`setup/`](setup/) folder provides automated batch and PowerShell scripts that handle all prerequisites on fresh or offline machines:
163: 
164: 1. **One-Click Dependency Installation**:
165:    - Double-click [`setup/install_dependencies.bat`](setup/install_dependencies.bat) (or run [`setup/install_dependencies.ps1`](setup/install_dependencies.ps1) in PowerShell).
166:    - *What this automates*:
167:      - Verifies Python installation; if Python is missing, automatically downloads and installs it silently with `Add to PATH` enabled via [`setup/setup_python.bat`](setup/setup_python.bat).
168:      - Installs or updates the PlatformIO CLI (`pio`) and adds its `Scripts` directory to the user environment `PATH`.
169:      - Ensures [`wokwigw.exe`](wokwigw.exe) is present in both `LocalConfig/` and `setup/`.
170:      - Pre-installs and verifies Espressif 32 toolchains (`toolchain-xtensa-esp-elf` and `framework-arduinoespressif32`).
171: 2. **Offline Installation (No Internet Required via GitHub Releases)**:
172:    - For campus lab machines without internet access, download the pre-packaged ~600MB localized toolchains archive (`platformio_cache.zip`) from **[GitHub Releases: wokwi_env_setup_script](https://github.com/b1tranger/wokwi_env_setup_script/releases/tag/platformio_cache.zip)**.
173:    - Direct Download: [platformio_cache.zip](https://github.com/b1tranger/wokwi_env_setup_script/releases/download/platformio_cache.zip/platformio_cache.zip)
174:    - Place the downloaded archive into [`setup/PlatformIO_Espressif_Offline_Installer/`](setup/PlatformIO_Espressif_Offline_Installer/).
175:    - Run [`setup/install_dependencies.bat`](setup/install_dependencies.bat) or [`setup/PlatformIO_Espressif_Offline_Installer/install_offline.bat`](setup/PlatformIO_Espressif_Offline_Installer/install_offline.bat). Both automatically detect the archive, extract the toolchains, and complete setup with zero network required.
176:    - For complete technical documentation on offline setup, see [`setup/SETUP_GUIDE.md`](setup/SETUP_GUIDE.md).
177: 3. **Reverting Changes & Uninstallation**:
178:    - If you ever need to revert firewall rules, stop gateway processes, and remove environment variables, run [`setup/uninstall_dependencies.bat`](setup/uninstall_dependencies.bat).

63: \begin{abstract}
64: Conventional Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices and web servers typically depend on full operating systems and power-hungry single-board computers or x86 processors. In this project, we implement a compact, low-power micro-NAS and static web server built around the ESP32-WROOM-32 microcontroller. Using FreeRTOS task separation, the hardware VSPI bus, and chunked HTTP streaming, the node operates as a local wireless file server capable of handling multipart file uploads, binary downloads, live storage telemetry, and static HTML/CSS web hosting without external cloud dependencies.
65: \end{abstract}
66: 
67: \begin{IEEEkeywords}
68: ESP32, Embedded Systems, FreeRTOS, Micro-NAS, VSPI, FAT32, Web Server.
69: \end{IEEEkeywords}
70: 
71: \section{\textbf{Introduction}}
72: Local data sharing and lightweight web hosting in embedded and field environments often do not justify the power draw or hardware cost of full Linux-based systems such as a Raspberry Pi, which typically consumes between 3 and 7 Watts under load. By comparison, an ESP32 microcontroller costs roughly \$4 and runs below 1 Watt while offering dual-core processing and integrated 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi.
73: 
74: In this work, we develop an embedded NAS and static website host on the ESP32 platform, validated using PlatformIO and a local Wokwi hardware simulation bridged to physical network interfaces via `wokwigw`. By interfacing a FAT32-formatted MicroSD card over the dedicated VSPI bus, our firmware supports browser-based file uploads, direct binary downloads, protected system directories, and static webpage delivery across local Wi-Fi and Ethernet networks without requiring client-side software installation.
75: 
76: \section{\textbf{Project Overview \& Objectives}}
77: 
78: \subsection{\textbf{Problem Statement \& Solution}}
79: Microcontrollers have strict memory limits—specifically 520 KB of internal SRAM on the ESP32, with roughly 320 KB available for the dynamic heap. Buffering entire multi-megabyte files in RAM during HTTP transfers causes immediate heap exhaustion and system resets. Additionally, blocking SD card block writes can stall network packet handling.
80: 
81: To solve both issues, our design separates network protocol handling on Core 0 from HTTP request routing and SD sector I/O on Core 1 via FreeRTOS. For file transfers, incoming multipart TCP payloads are accumulated into a fixed 4,096-byte sector-aligned RAM buffer before being flushed to the FAT32 card, keeping runtime memory overhead constant regardless of file size.
82: 
83: \subsection{\textbf{Core Objectives}}
84: \begin{itemize}
85:     \item Build a localized, browser-accessible file storage system on an ESP32 microcontroller using the hardware VSPI interface.
86:     \item Develop a responsive web dashboard with live storage metrics, recursive file listing (`/api/files`), and write-protection for system assets.
87:     \item Support dual-mode operation: serving binary file downloads alongside static HTML5/CSS/JS web pages from the `/www/` directory.
88:     \item Verify system stability, memory usage, and multi-device LAN accessibility across both simulated and physical network bridges.
89: \end{itemize}
90: 
91: \section{\textbf{System Architecture \& Working Principle}}
92: 
93: \subsection{\textbf{Key Components \& Specifications}}
94: The system combines hardware peripherals and firmware modules tuned for constrained SRAM environments:
95: \begin{itemize}
96:     \item \textbf{Microcontroller:} ESP32-WROOM-32 (Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 microprocessor at 240 MHz, 520 KB SRAM, and 4 MB SPI Flash).
97:     \item \textbf{Storage Subsystem:} MicroSD card module formatted in FAT32, connected to the VSPI hardware peripheral (GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23) and clocked at 4 MHz for reliable block-write timing.
98:     \item \textbf{Network Subsystem:} Integrated 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi radio running the LwIP TCP/IP stack and the native Arduino-ESP32 `WebServer` on port 80, bridged to host LAN/hotspot interfaces on port 9080 during simulation.
99:     \item \textbf{Firmware Memory Management:} Default web interfaces (`/www/fileserver.html`, `/www/index.html`) and sample reports are converted at build time into `PROGMEM` byte arrays (`default_assets.h`) and streamed via `FPSTR()` directly from Flash ROM.
100: \end{itemize}
101: 
102: \subsection{\textbf{Working Method \& Execution Flow}}
103: The firmware executes through a two-phase initialization and runtime sequence:
104: \begin{enumerate}
105:     \item \textbf{Phase 1 (Storage Initialization \& Seeding):} The firmware explicitly binds the VSPI pins (`SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, 5)`) and mounts the FAT32 volume. It verifies or creates `/default`, `/www`, and `/uploads`, calculates total and used storage (`SD.totalBytes()` and `SD.usedBytes()`), and seeds default assets from Flash ROM if they are missing.
106:     \item \textbf{Phase 2 (Network \& HTTP Service):} After associating with the Wi-Fi access point, the node binds REST and static routes (`/`, `/site`, `/api/files`, `/get`, `/upload`, `/delete`) and starts listening on port 80. A FreeRTOS diagnostic task (`xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`) runs stream-drained loopback checks on Core 1 to verify endpoint health without leaking open sockets.
107: \end{enumerate}
108: 
109: \section{\textbf{Implementation Procedures}}
110: 
111: \subsection{\textbf{Circuit Setup \& Interface Pinout}}
112: The MicroSD breakout board connects directly to the ESP32 hardware VSPI pins as listed in Table~\ref{tab:pinout}.
113: 
114: \begin{table}[htbp]
115: \caption{ESP32 to MicroSD Module Pinout}
116: \begin{center}
117: \begin{tabular}{llll}
118: \toprule
119: \textbf{ESP32 Pin} & \textbf{SD Module} & \textbf{Function} & \textbf{Description} \\
120: \midrule
121: 3V3 & VCC & Power & Regulated 3.3V Supply \\
122: GND & GND & Ground & Common Ground Reference \\
123: GPIO 5 & CS & Chip Select & Active-Low SPI Slave Select \\
124: GPIO 23 & MOSI/DI & Data Input & Master Out, Slave In \\
125: GPIO 19 & MISO/DO & Data Output & Master In, Slave Out \\
126: GPIO 18 & SCK/CLK & Clock & SPI Synchronization Clock \\
127: \bottomrule
128: \end{tabular}
129: \label{tab:pinout}
130: \end{center}
131: \end{table}
132: 
133: \subsection{\textbf{Firmware Implementation}}
134: The firmware routes HTTP requests and streams files in 4 KB sector-aligned blocks using the core setup shown below:
135: 
136: \begin{lstlisting}
137: #include <WiFi.h>
138: #include <WebServer.h>
139: #include <SPI.h>
140: #include <SD.h>
141: 
142: #define SD_CS_PIN 5
143: #define UPLOAD_BUF_SIZE 4096
144: 
145: WebServer server(80);
146: static uint8_t uploadWriteBuffer[UPLOAD_BUF_SIZE];
147: 
148: void setup() {
149:     Serial.begin(115200);
150:     SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, SD_CS_PIN);
151:     if (!SD.begin(SD_CS_PIN, SPI, 4000000)) {
152:         Serial.println("[ERROR] SD Init Failed");
153:         return;
154:     }
155:     WiFi.begin("SSID", "PASSWORD");
156:     while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) {
157:         delay(200);
158:     }
159:     server.on("/", HTTP_GET, handleRoot);
160:     server.on("/site", HTTP_GET, handleSite);
161:     server.on("/api/files", HTTP_GET, handleApiFiles);
162:     server.on("/get", HTTP_GET, handleDownload);
163:     server.on("/upload", HTTP_POST, handleUploadComplete, handleFileUpload);
164:     server.on("/delete", HTTP_GET, handleDelete);
165:     server.begin();
166: }
167: 
168: void loop() {
169:     server.handleClient();
170: }
171: \end{lstlisting}
172: 
173: \section{\textbf{Project Scope and Limitations}}
174: 
175: \subsection{\textbf{Electrical Stability \& Memory Constraints}}
176: On physical hardware, MicroSD flash page writes can draw transient current spikes up to 200 mA. Combined with Wi-Fi transmission bursts, peak current demand can exceed 500 mA, which may trigger brownout resets if powered over weak USB cables. Placing a 10 $\mu$F electrolytic capacitor and a 0.1 $\mu$F ceramic decoupling capacitor across VCC and GND stabilizes the 3.3V rail. On the software side, keeping HTTP headers and TCP buffers active leaves roughly 250--300 KB of usable heap, limiting practical concurrency to 4--8 simultaneous browser clients. Additionally, unencrypted HTTP is used rather than HTTPS because TLS handshakes consume roughly 45 KB of heap per session and cannot use trusted public certificates on local private IP subnets.
177: 
178: \subsection{\textbf{Simulation vs. Physical Hardware Comparison}}
179: Table~\ref{tab:comparison} summarizes the practical differences observed between our local Wokwi simulation workspace and physical ESP32 hardware deployment.
180: 
181: \begin{table}[htbp]
182: \caption{Simulation vs. Physical Environment Comparison}
183: \begin{center}
184: \begin{tabular}{p{2.0cm} p{2.8cm} p{2.8cm}}
185: \toprule
186: \textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Wokwi Local Simulation} & \textbf{Physical Hardware} \\
187: \midrule
188: Storage Medium & Host-synced virtual FAT32 volume capped at 256 MB (`writeback = true`). & Physical MicroSD card (4 GB--32 GB) with real flash wear and sector latency. \\
189: Network Access & Routed via `wokwigw` bridge (`0.0.0.0:9080` $\rightarrow$ `10.13.37.2:80`). & Direct 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi router association or standalone SoftAP (`192.168.4.1`). \\
190: SPI Clocking & Clocked at 4 MHz to avoid virtual bus timing errors during block writes. & Supports 4 MHz--25 MHz depending on jumper wire length and capacitance. \\
191: \bottomrule
192: \end{tabular}
193: \label{tab:comparison}
194: \end{center}
195: \end{table}
196: 
197: \section{\textbf{Conclusion}}
198: This project demonstrates that an ESP32 microcontroller can reliably serve as an energy-efficient, zero-install edge NAS and static web host. By pairing FreeRTOS dual-core task isolation with 4 KB sector-aligned upload buffering, `PROGMEM` asset storage, and write-protected system directories, the firmware avoids heap exhaustion while maintaining responsive file transfers across desktop and mobile browsers. In off-grid deployments, switching the Wi-Fi driver to SoftAP mode allows the node to operate as a self-contained wireless file hub without an external router or host computer.

48: \begin{abstract}
49: Traditional Network Attached Storage (NAS) units and web hosting servers rely on high-power application processors, which consume substantial energy and require complex operating systems. This project designs a low-power, solid-state micro-NAS and web server node built around the ESP32 microcontroller. Utilizing FreeRTOS, a dedicated hardware SPI/SDMMC interface, and asynchronous TCP handling, the system functions as a localized wireless file storage server capable of hosting static web pages, client-side Single-Page Applications (SPAs), and sensor dashboards.
50: \end{abstract}
51: 
52: \begin{IEEEkeywords}
53: ESP32, Embedded Systems, FreeRTOS, Micro-NAS, IoT, Web Hosting.
54: \end{IEEEkeywords}
55: 
56: \section{Introduction}
57: Embedded systems and the Internet of Things (IoT) demand lightweight, energy-efficient data management alternatives. Conventional Network Attached Storage (NAS) units and web hosting servers rely on power-hungry single-board computers (such as Raspberry Pi) or x86 servers drawing 15 to 60 Watts. This project demonstrates that an ultra-low-cost (\$4), low-power ($<1$ Watt) ESP32 dual-core microcontroller can autonomously function as an air-gapped, zero-trust edge NAS and static web host. By interfacing a FAT32 MicroSD card over the hardware SPI bus, our firmware delivers multipart file uploads, chunked downloads, dynamic file deletion, real-time storage telemetry, and static HTML5 website hosting directly to desktop and mobile browsers via a localized network bridge.
58: 
59: \section{Project Overview \& Objectives}
60: 
61: \subsection{Problem Statement \& Solution}
62: The system targets low-power edge computing. By leveraging the dual-core Xtensa architecture of the ESP32, Core 0 manages the Wi-Fi/TCP stack (LwIP) while Core 1 handles file system operations via FreeRTOS. This task partitioning prevents network timeouts during SD card read and write loops.
63: 
64: \subsection{Core Objectives}
65: \begin{itemize}
66:     \item Implement a wireless, localized file storage architecture on an embedded platform.
67:     \item Design an intuitive HTTP dashboard for file manipulation (directory structure, downloading files, free/used storage metrics).
68:     \item Enable dual-purpose functionality: serving file streams alongside static web assets (HTML5/CSS/JavaScript).
69:     \item Evaluate system throughput, memory footprints, and architectural constraints.
70: \end{itemize}
71: 
72: \section{System Architecture \& Working Principle}
73: 
74: \subsection{Key Components \& Specifications}
75: The system architecture integrates hardware modules and software subsystems designed for maximum efficiency under constrained memory resources:
76: \begin{itemize}
77:     \item \textbf{Microcontroller:} ESP32-WROOM-32 featuring an Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 microprocessor operating at 240 MHz with 520 KB internal SRAM.
78:     \item \textbf{Storage Subsystem:} MicroSD card module formatted with FAT32, interfaced via the dedicated VSPI hardware peripheral (GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23).
79:     \item \textbf{Network Subsystem:} On-chip 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi transceiver running an asynchronous LwIP TCP/IP stack and ESPAsyncWebServer daemon.
80:     \item \textbf{Firmware Memory Management:} HTML UI templates optimized via PROGMEM and FPSTR strings to stream directly from flash ROM, preserving internal SRAM heap.
81: \end{itemize}
82: 
83: \subsection{Working Method \& Execution Flow}
84: The system operates through a dual-phase execution pipeline:
85: \begin{enumerate}
86:     \item \textbf{Phase 1 (Storage Boot):} The firmware explicitly binds the VSPI bus (`SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, 5)`) and mounts the FAT32 filesystem. It computes storage capacity metrics (`SD.totalBytes()` and `SD.usedBytes()`) and dynamically seeds default assets including `/www/index.html` and `/lab_report.txt`.
87:     \item \textbf{Phase 2 (Network & Web Server Boot):} The node connects to Wi-Fi, binds REST endpoints (`/`, `/site`, `/get`, `/upload`, `/delete`), and starts the asynchronous web server daemon on port 80. Concurrently, a FreeRTOS diagnostic worker (`xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`) runs asynchronous loopback validations on Core 1.
88: \end{enumerate}
89: 
90: \section{Implementation Procedures}
91: 
92: \subsection{Circuit Setup \& Interface Pinout}
93: The MicroSD module connects to the hardware VSPI bus as detailed in Table I.
94:

96: \caption{ESP32 to MicroSD Module Pinout}
97: \begin{center}
98: \begin{tabular}{llll}
99: \toprule
100: \textbf{ESP32 Pin} & \textbf{SD Module} & \textbf{Function} & \textbf{Description} \\

44: ## 1. Delivery Strategy for Non-Native English Speakers
45: 
46: * **Keep Sentences Short (Subject + Verb + Object)**: Avoid dense compound clauses. Instead of saying *"Considering the severe computational and volatile memory limitations imposed by the Xtensa architecture, we utilized a chunked streaming transfer mechanism,"* say:
47:   > *"The ESP32 has small memory. So, our firmware streams incoming files in small 2 KB chunks directly into the SD card."*
48: * **The "Look, Point, Explain" Rule**: When presenting slides or demonstrating the live software, do not look down at paper scripts. Point directly to the diagram, button, storage meter, or serial log on the screen, state what it is, and explain its hardware role in one clear sentence.
49: * **Active Laptop Operator Coordination**:
50:   * The designated speaker focuses 100% on oral delivery and maintaining eye contact with the evaluators.
51:   * A second team member operates the laptop, advancing slides and executing demo actions (clicking **Choose File**, **Upload**, **Download**, **Delete**, and switching browser tabs) without the speaker needing to turn around or lose momentum.
52: * **Pacing & Breathing**: Non-native speakers often speak rapidly when nervous. Maintain an intentional speaking cadence of **110–120 words per minute**. Take a full 1-to-2 second pause between slide transitions to allow evaluators to read the visual headers.
53: * **Mutual Fallback Protocol**: If a speaker forgets a specific technical keyword (such as *"PROGMEM"*, *"VSPI"*, or *"multipart chunk"*), the operating partner calmly mentions the keyword to keep the rhythm unbroken.
54:

69: 
70: ### Part 1: Introduction, Scope & Simulation Platform Selection (Speaker 1 — 2.5 Minutes)
71: 
72: #### 1.1 The Presentation Hook
73: * **Conduct**: Begin with an energetic contrast. Point to an image of a bulky, expensive commercial NAS unit, a desktop router, or an x86 server.
74: * **Spoken Narrative**:
75:   > *"Good morning, respected teachers and peers. Traditional Network Attached Storage (NAS) units and web servers consume 15 to 60 Watts of continuous power and cost thousands of takas. Today, our team proves that an ultra-low-cost, 4-dollar ESP32 microprocessor can autonomously act as an air-gapped, zero-cloud local file storage node and static website host, consuming less than 1 Watt of power."*
76: 
77: #### 1.2 Project & Team Identity
78: * **Conduct**: Transition to the formal academic slide. Introduce your course code, course title, faculty advisors, and team members clearly.
79: * **Spoken Narrative**:
80:   > *"This project is submitted for CSE0611324: Microprocessors, Microcontrollers and Assembly Language Lab under the guidance of our honorable lecturers, Tahmina Yeasmin Lima ma'am and Abrar Mahbub Tanim sir. Our team members are Jannatul Ferdus, Gaus Saraf Murady, and Sadia Islam."*
81: 
82: #### 1.3 Project Scope & Real-World Objectives
83: * **Conduct**: Point out the dual-purpose nature of the system.
84: * **Spoken Narrative**:
85:   > *"Our scope is twofold:*
86:   > * *First, create a localized, wireless Network Attached Storage (NAS) node that handles file uploads, chunked downloads, and directory management without any external computer software.*
87:   > * *Second, serve static HTML5 web assets directly from raw block storage, acting as an offline documentation server.*
88:   > * *Most importantly, this system operates entirely air-gapped—requiring zero cloud connections, zero external subscriptions, and zero maintenance."*
89: 
90: #### 1.4 Selection of Simulation Platform (Why Wokwi over Proteus/Tinkercad)
91: * **Conduct**: Address simulation feasibility directly to preempt common evaluator questions.
92: * **Spoken Narrative**:
93:   > *"To validate our design, we evaluated multiple simulators. Tinkercad cannot simulate 32-bit microcontrollers or Wi-Fi. Proteus can simulate an SD card over SPI, but it completely lacks the ESP32 Wi-Fi and TCP/IP protocol stack. We chose Wokwi because it uses WebAssembly to execute raw compiled machine instructions, accurately models hardware SPI peripheral lines, and simulates the complete LwIP networking stack."*
94: * **Handoff**: *"Now, my teammate will explain our budget, prove technical feasibility, and demonstrate the working live system."*

98: ### Part 2: Budget, Architecture & Live Demonstration (Speaker 2 — 4.0 Minutes)
99: 
100: #### 2.1 Financial Feasibility (Bill of Materials under 900 BDT)
101: * **Conduct**: Present the component sourcing table. Highlight that every part is standard, low-cost, and readily available in local electronics markets.
102: * **Spoken Narrative**:
103:   > *"When designing embedded systems, cost is paramount. As shown on our Bill of Materials, the physical deployment requires only four items:*
104:   > * *An ESP32 DevKit V1 board: approximately 400 Taka.*
105:   > * *A MicroSD SPI breakout adapter: around 80 Taka.*
106:   > * *A Class 10 MicroSD card: around 250 Taka.*
107:   > * *A set of short Dupont jumper wires: 20 Taka.*
108:   > * *The total hardware budget is under 900 Bangladeshi Taka—roughly 7 US dollars."*
109: 
110: #### 2.2 Technical & Computational Feasibility
111: * **Conduct**: Explain why a 400-Taka chip can handle high-throughput file transfers without crashing.
112: * **Spoken Narrative**:
113:   > *"Is a 4-dollar chip computationally feasible for this role? Yes, due to three architectural engineering decisions:*
114:   > * *1. Symmetric Dual-Core Partitioning: The ESP32 has two independent 240 MHz Xtensa CPU cores. Using FreeRTOS, Core 0 runs the LwIP Wi-Fi stack, while Core 1 handles SPI storage read and write operations. Because disk latency never blocks network interrupts, web connections never drop.*
115:   > * *2. Streaming Memory Guarantee: The ESP32 has roughly 300 KB of usable heap. To prevent out-of-memory kernel panics, we never buffer entire files in RAM. Instead, our multipart upload and download routines stream incoming network packets directly into SD card blocks in 2 KB buffers. Whether a file is 10 KB or 100 MB, RAM consumption remains fixed at just 2 KB.*
116:   > * *3. Flash Memory Optimization: Our glassmorphic HTML and CSS layouts are placed into 4 MB Flash ROM using the `PROGMEM` keyword and streamed via `FPSTR()`. This keeps RAM completely clear for network operations."*
117:

144: ### Part 3: Real-World Impact, Challenges, Hardware Realities & Conclusion (Speaker 3 — 2.5 Minutes)
145: 
146: #### 3.1 Real-Life Problems Solved & Market Demand (Bangladesh Context)
147: * **Conduct**: Speak with conviction about local, practical use cases.
148: * **Spoken Narrative**:
149:   > *"Where does this system create real-world value?*
150:   > * *Disaster & Flood Relief: During monsoon floods in rural Bangladesh, cellular towers often lose power or become congested. This battery-operated node can broadcast emergency evacuation maps, medical guides, and shelter information locally over Wi-Fi.*
151:   > * *Air-Gapped Field Data Logging: In remote agricultural stations or industrial plants, microcontrollers can log environmental sensors to the SD card; engineers can walk up, connect locally, and download logs without needing internet cables.*
152:   > * *Rural Education & Clinics: Commercial cloud storage (AWS, Google Drive) requires foreign currency and continuous high-speed broadband. A 900-Taka node can store digitized textbooks, offline encyclopedias, and local clinic records for an entire village classroom."*
153: 
154: #### 3.2 Key Debugging Challenges & Engineering Solutions
155: * **Conduct**: Highlight how the team identified and resolved low-level simulation bugs. Evaluators value these specific engineering problem-solving details.
156: * **Spoken Narrative**:
157:   > *"During development, we encountered and resolved four major technical bottlenecks:*
158:   > * *1. The Wokwi D-Pin Silkscreen Bug: In `diagram.json`, declaring `esp:5` caused silent SPI connection failures because Wokwi's pin model requires the physical silkscreen label `esp:D5`. Correcting this restored the SPI bus connection.*
159:   > * *2. The SPI Clock Schema Mismatch: Standard breakout boards label the clock line as `CLK`, but Wokwi's part schema strictly requires `SCK`. Aligning this ensured proper bus synchronization.*
160:   > * *3. Library Version Deprecation: Newer ESP32 Arduino Cores removed legacy `mbedtls` MD5 functions, breaking older async libraries. We transitioned to the native, lightweight `WebServer.h` library, eliminating external dependencies completely.*
161:   > * *4. Multi-Interface Firewall & Gateway Bridging: To allow external lab computers and smartphones to access the node without connection timeouts, we authored `setup_firewall.bat` with auto-elevation to open inbound TCP 9080, and configured `wokwigw.exe` to bridge `0.0.0.0:9080` into virtual IP `10.13.37.2:80`."*
162: 
163: #### 3.3 Simulation vs. Physical Hardware Realities
164: * **Conduct**: Explain what must be taken into account when moving from the virtual canvas to real physical hardware.
165: * **Spoken Narrative**:
166:   > *"A simulation assumes ideal electrical conditions. To transition this code to physical silicon, we designed for two physical constraints:*
167:   > * *Power Rail Brownouts: Wi-Fi data bursts draw sudden current spikes over 300 mA, which can trip the ESP32's internal brownout detector. We mitigate this on breadboards by placing a 10 to 100 µF decoupling capacitor across the 3.3V rail.*
168:   > * *Bus Parasitic Capacitance: In simulation, wires have zero resistance. On physical breadboards, loose jumper wires cause signal degradation; we mitigate this by capping the SPI bus clock frequency at 10 MHz and keeping wires under 15 cm."*
169: 
170: #### 3.4 Future Roadmap & Final Conclusion
171: * **Conduct**: End on a forward-looking, confident note.
172: * **Spoken Narrative**:
173:   > *"For future work, we plan to implement:*
174:   > * *SoftAP Mode (`192.168.4.1`): Enabling the ESP32 to broadcast its own independent Wi-Fi access point, eliminating the need for an external Wi-Fi router entirely.*
175:   > * *ESP32-S3 USB Host Integration: Evaluating the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to interface standard USB thumb drives and external hard drives directly.*
176:   > * *Battery Management: Powering the node via an 18650 power bank enclosure for over 20 hours of continuous off-grid operation.*
177:   > 
178:   > *In conclusion, we have designed, simulated, and validated a complete, energy-efficient micro-NAS and web node for under 900 Taka. Thank you for your time and attention. We are now ready to answer your questions."*

182: ## 4. Evaluator Q&A Defense Quick-Reference
183: 
184: Have this reference sheet open during evaluator questions. Each team member should be prepared to handle their designated technical domain.
185: 
186: ### Q1: Why use an ESP32 instead of a Raspberry Pi? (Speaker 1)
187: * **Rebuttal**: Cost and power. A Raspberry Pi costs $45–$75 and draws 3 to 7 Watts of power. The ESP32 costs $4, draws less than 0.5 Watts, boots in under 500 milliseconds, and has no complex Linux OS vulnerabilities or patch cycles to manage.
188: 
189: ### Q2: What happens if an uploaded file exceeds the ESP32 RAM? (Speaker 2)
190: * **Rebuttal**: It uploads safely without crashing. The firmware never buffers the whole file in RAM. It uses a streaming multipart parser that receives 1.4 KB TCP packets and flushes them immediately across the SPI bus into SD card blocks before accepting the next packet. RAM usage remains constant at 2 KB.
191: 
192: ### Q3: Is the HTTP server running on the PC or inside the ESP32? (Speaker 2)
193: * **Rebuttal**: It is 100% internal and native to the ESP32 C++ firmware (`WebServer server(80)`). The PC is not running Apache or Nginx. In simulation, `wokwigw.exe` is only a transparent Layer-2/3 packet forwarder bridging host ports to the virtual MAC address.
194: 
195: ### Q4: Why choose SPI mode over 4-bit SDMMC for the SD card? (Speaker 3)
196: * **Rebuttal**: Pin safety and hardware compatibility. 4-bit SDMMC requires 6 pins, including GPIO 12, which is an internal strapping pin that can brick bootup if pulled high at power-on. SPI mode requires only 4 pins, has universal support across cheap breakout boards, and matches our approved proposal pinout table (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`).
197: 
198: ### Q5: How does this system operate in a disaster zone without a Wi-Fi router? (Speaker 3)
199: * **Rebuttal**: Using native SoftAP mode (`WiFi.softAP("ESP32-Edge-NAS", "12345678")`). The ESP32 broadcasts its own Wi-Fi SSID and assigns IP addresses via an internal DHCP server. Anyone can connect directly to `http://192.168.4.1/` without an external router or internet connection.
200: 
201: ### Q6: How does the file server allow 2 computers in the lab to share files like LocalSend Web? (Speaker 2)
202: * **Rebuttal**: LocalSend Web starts a temporary web server on one PC so other machines can visit it in a browser to upload or download files without installing an app. Our ESP32 NAS operates on the exact same zero-install browser principle. However, instead of running as a desktop app on PC hardware, our system is an independent embedded hardware appliance: files are committed directly to MicroSD FAT32 blocks via VSPI, and both computers are equal clients to the ESP32 node.
203: 
204: ### Q7: What if the campus network has Client/AP Isolation enabled? (Speaker 1)
205: * **Rebuttal**: If the university router blocks PC-to-PC communication, the host machine turns on **Windows Mobile Hotspot** (`Settings > Mobile hotspot`). Windows creates a local wireless network assigning the host `192.168.137.1`. The second computer connects to this hotspot and accesses `http://192.168.137.1:9080/`, completely bypassing campus network isolation.
206: 
207: ### Q8: Why does wokwigw work across LAN, and why was setup_firewall.bat created? (Speaker 3)
208: * **Rebuttal**: When `wokwigw.exe` is started with `--forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80`, it binds to socket `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`), listening on all network adapters (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Hotspot). Because Windows Defender Firewall blocks unsolicited inbound TCP traffic by default, we created `setup_firewall.bat` with auto-UAC elevation to open inbound port 9080 across all profiles, ensuring peer computers can connect without timeouts.
209:

212: ## 5. Pre-Presentation Rehearsal Checklist
213: 
214: 1. **Firewall Rule Enabled**: Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator once on your presentation laptop.
215: 2. **Local Bridge Running in Background**: Open PowerShell in [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) and launch the gateway prior to stepping to the podium:
216:    ```powershell
217:    .\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80
218:    ```
219: 3. **Pre-Compile Firmware**: Build the PlatformIO project beforehand (`Ctrl + Alt + B`) so you do not wait for cross-compilation during the 10-minute presentation window.
220: 4. **Browser Tab Ready**: Have Chrome or Edge pre-opened to `http://localhost:9080/`.
221: 5. **Test Payload Prepared**: Have a small, clean PDF, `.asm` file, or image file (under 2 MB) ready on the desktop for the live upload demonstration.
222: 6. **Mobile Hotspot Verified (Optional Backup)**: Enable Windows Mobile Hotspot so you can demonstrate mobile access at `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` if Wi-Fi in the lab room is unstable.

92: ## 1. Executive Pitch & Project Scope
93: 
94: ### 1.1 The 30-Second Elevator Pitch
95: > *"Traditional Network Attached Storage (NAS) units and web servers rely on power-hungry single-board computers (like Raspberry Pi) or x86 servers drawing 15 to 60 Watts. In this project, we prove that an ultra-low-cost ($4), low-power (<1 Watt) ESP32 dual-core microcontroller can autonomously act as an air-gapped, zero-trust edge NAS and static web host. Interfacing a FAT32 MicroSD card over the hardware SPI bus, our firmware delivers full multipart file uploads, chunked downloads, dynamic file deletion, real-time storage telemetry, and static HTML5 website hosting directly to desktop browsers via a local network bridge."*
96: 
97: ### 1.2 Project Scope & Real-World Goals
98: 1. **Air-Gapped Field Data Logging**: In remote industrial sites, environmental sensors can log high-frequency telemetry onto an SD card; field engineers can walk up, connect via local Wi-Fi, and download data or manage logs through an intuitive web UI without any internet connection.
99: 2. **Decentralized Emergency Web Node**: In disaster-relief zones or off-grid scenarios, this node can broadcast emergency static documentation, evacuation maps, and survival guides stored directly on physical flash media.
100: 3. **Ultra-Low Cost & Zero Maintenance**: No spinning hard drives, no noisy fans, zero Linux OS kernel overhead, and instant boot times (< 1 second) with zero vulnerability to common operating system zero-day exploits.

68: ## 3. Analysis & Key Insights (Root Cause Investigation)
69: 
70: ### 3.1 The Architecture of `henryxiaoyang.realtime-tex` and `rtex`
71: `realtime-tex` (`rtex`) provides millisecond-level live LaTeX rendering by keeping a warm, persistent **LuaLaTeX** process alive in the background with the document preamble pre-loaded. When the author edits text, `rtex` does not recompile the entire document; instead, it re-typesets *only* the specific paragraph currently being edited in ~1 millisecond using LuaLaTeX callbacks.
72: 
73: However, **`rtex` is only an orchestration daemon and bridge**—it does not bundle the TeX compiler binaries, macro packages, or fonts itself. It strictly delegates all compilation passes to `lualatex`.
74: 
75: ### 3.2 Verification via `rtex doctor`
76: Directly invoking the bundled diagnostic tool revealed the exact failure point:
77: ```powershell
78: & "C:\Users\gsmur\AppData\Roaming\Antigravity IDE\User\globalStorage\henryxiaoyang.realtime-tex\rtex-release\v0.0.7\bin\rtex.exe" doctor
79: ```
80: **Diagnostic Output:**
81: ```text
82: rtex 0.0.7
83: support files: C:\Users\gsmur\AppData\Roaming\Antigravity IDE\User\globalStorage\henryxiaoyang.realtime-tex\rtex-release\v0.0.7\share\rtex\tex
84: lualatex: missing (lualatex not found on PATH (source build/texlive.env or set RTEX_TEXLIVE_BIN))
85: ```
86: 
87: ### 3.3 The Missing System Component: LuaLaTeX
88: Because the host machine lacked a TeX distribution (TeX Live or MiKTeX), `rtex` failed to spawn the compiler process when initiating the live preview panel.
89:

97: - **[`install.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/windows-miktex-installer/install.bat)**: Double-clickable batch launcher for Windows Explorer. Handles elevation detection and passes execution to PowerShell with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`.
98: - **[`install.ps1`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/windows-miktex-installer/install.ps1)**: Core automation script featuring colored logging, idempotency checks, dual installation backends, binary path resolution, and editor integration testing.
99: - **[`verify.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/windows-miktex-installer/verify.bat)** & **[`verify.ps1`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/windows-miktex-installer/verify.ps1)**: Non-destructive health check tool verifying binary detection, on-the-fly download configuration, sample LaTeX compilation, and `rtex doctor` status.
100: - **[`test/sample.tex`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/windows-miktex-installer/test/sample.tex)**: Multi-package test document using `amsmath`, `listings`, and `booktabs` to validate automated package fetching.

141: ### Firmware Architecture (`Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp`):
142: - **Phase 1**: Hardware VSPI mounting, automatic seeding of `/www/index.html` and `/lab_report.txt`, and file enumeration.
143: - **Phase 2**: Asynchronous WebServer handling root dashboard (`/`), static hosting (`/site`), streaming downloads (`/get`), multipart uploads (`/upload`), and background auto-diagnostics running on FreeRTOS Core 1.

High-Yield Evaluator Q&A Defense Quick-Reference\n\n| Question | Core Engineering Defense / Rebuttal | Key Technical Keywords |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| **Q1: Why use an ESP32 instead of a Raspberry Pi?** | A Raspberry Pi costs \\$45–\\$75, draws 3–7 Watts, and requires a full Linux OS with security patch cycles. The ESP32 costs \\$4 (~400 BDT), consumes < 0.5 Watts, boots instantly (< 500 ms), and runs bare-metal FreeRTOS with zero OS vulnerabilities. | Cost, Sub-1W, FreeRTOS, Instant Boot |\n| **Q2: What happens if an uploaded file exceeds the ESP32 RAM?** | It uploads safely without crashing. We never buffer the full file in memory. The firmware uses a streaming multipart parser that writes incoming 2 KB TCP packets directly to SD sectors before accepting the next packet. Heap overhead remains constant at ~2 KB. | Constant 2 KB Heap, `server.upload()`, Direct Flush |\n| **Q3: Is the HTTP server running on the PC or inside the ESP32?** | It is 100% native to the ESP32 C++ firmware (`WebServer server(80)`). The PC runs no web server software (no Apache, Nginx, or Node.js). In simulation, `wokwigw.exe` is merely a transparent Layer 2/3 packet bridge forwarding host port 9080 to the virtual ESP32. | Native `WebServer.h`, Packet Bridge |\n| **Q4: Why choose SPI mode over 4-bit SDMMC for the SD card?** | 4-bit SDMMC requires 6 pins, including GPIO 12 which is an internal strapping pin that can brick bootup if pulled high at power-on. SPI mode requires only 4 pins (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`), avoids strapping pins, and is 100% supported by low-cost breakout modules. | Strapping Pin GPIO 12, 4-Pin VSPI |\n| **Q5: How does this system operate in a disaster zone without a Wi-Fi router?** | Using native **SoftAP Mode** (`WiFi.softAP(\"ESP32-Edge-NAS\")`). The ESP32 broadcasts its own Wi-Fi SSID and assigns client IPs via an internal DHCP server on `192.168.4.1`. Clients connect directly to the node without an external router or internet. | SoftAP Mode, DHCP, `192.168.4.1`, Air-Gapped |\n| **Q6: How does the file server allow 2 computers in the lab to share files like LocalSend Web?** | LocalSend Web runs a temporary browser server on a PC. Our project does the same thing on an embedded microprocessor. Because `wokwigw` binds to `0.0.0.0:9080` and Windows Firewall port 9080 is open, any other PC or phone on the same lab network accesses the shared storage via browser without software installation. | Zero-Install, `0.0.0.0:9080`, Multi-Device LAN |\n| **Q7: What if the campus network has Client/AP Isolation enabled?** | If campus Wi-Fi blocks inter-device communication, the host laptop turns on **Windows Mobile Hotspot**. Windows creates an independent Wi-Fi network assigning the host `192.168.137.1`. 186: void collectFilesRecursively(File dir, std::vector<StorageItem> &items,
187:                              int depth = 0) {
188:   if (!dir || !dir.isDirectory() || depth > 3)
189:     return;
190: 
191:   File file = dir.openNextFile();
192:   while (file) {
193:     if (file.isDirectory()) {
194:       collectFilesRecursively(file, items, depth + 1);
195:     } else {
196:       String fullPath = String(file.name());
197:       if (!fullPath.startsWith("/"))
198:         fullPath = "/" + fullPath;
199: 
200:       // Skip root /lab_report.txt if /default/lab_report.txt exists to avoid
201:       // duplicate rows
202:       if (fullPath == "/lab_report.txt" &&
203:           SD.exists("/default/lab_report.txt")) {
204:         file = dir.openNextFile();
205:         continue;
206:       }
207: 
208:       StorageItem item;
209:       item.path = fullPath;
210:       item.size = file.size();
211:       item.isProtected = isProtectedPath(fullPath);
212:       items.push_back(item);
213:     }
214:     file = dir.openNextFile();
215:   }
216: }

218: // High-performance streaming of SD card files to client in 1024-byte block chunks.
219: // Eliminates WebServer::streamFile() CPU byte-by-byte bottlenecks and socket deadlocks.
220: static void streamSDFile(File &file, const String &contentType,
221:                          bool isAttachment = false,
222:                          const String &downloadFilename = "") {
223:   if (!file || file.isDirectory()) {
224:     if (file)
225:       file.close();
226:     server.sendHeader("Connection", "close");
227:     server.send(404, "text/plain", "File Not Found");
228:     WiFiClient client = server.client();
229:     client.flush();
230:     client.stop();
231:     return;
232:   }
233: 
234:   size_t totalSize = file.size();
235:   file.setBufferSize(1024);
236: 
237:   server.sendHeader("Cache-Control", "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate");
238:   server.sendHeader("Pragma", "no-cache");
239:   server.sendHeader("Expires", "-1");
240:   if (isAttachment && downloadFilename.length() > 0) {
241:     server.sendHeader("Content-Disposition",
242:                       "attachment; filename=\"" + downloadFilename + "\"");
243:   }
244:   server.sendHeader("Content-Length", String(totalSize));
245:   server.sendHeader("Connection", "close");
246:   server.setContentLength(totalSize);
247:   server.send(200, contentType, "");
248: 
249:   WiFiClient client = server.client();
250:   uint8_t buffer[1024];
251:   size_t remaining = totalSize;
252: 
253:   while (client.connected() && remaining > 0) {
254:     size_t toRead = (remaining > sizeof(buffer)) ? sizeof(buffer) : remaining;
255:     size_t nRead = file.read(buffer, toRead);
256:     if (nRead == 0) {
257:       break;
258:     }
259:     size_t nWritten = client.write(buffer, nRead);
260:     if (nWritten == 0) {
261:       break;
262:     }
263:     remaining -= nWritten;
264:     vTaskDelay(1);
265:   }
266: 
267:   file.close();
268:   client.flush();
269:   client.stop();
270: }

550:           f.write(EMBEDDED_ASSETS[i].data + writtenTotal, chunk);
551:           writtenTotal += chunk;
552:         }
553:         f.flush();
554:         f.close();
555:         File htmlFile = SD.open("/www/index.html", FILE_READ);
556:         if (htmlFile && htmlFile.size() > 0) {
557:           streamSDFile(htmlFile, "text/html");
558:           return;
559:         }
560:         if (htmlFile)
561:           htmlFile.close();
562:       }
563:       // Direct Flash ROM fallback if SD write failed
564:       server.sendHeader("Connection", "close");
565:       server.send_P(200, "text/html", (PGM_P)EMBEDDED_ASSETS[i].data,
566:                     EMBEDDED_ASSETS[i].size);
567:       WiFiClient client = server.client();
568:       client.flush();
569:       client.stop();
570:       return;
571:     }
572:   }
573: 
574:   server.sendHeader("Connection", "close");
575:   server.send(404, "text/plain",
576:               "Static Site Not Found on MicroSD (/www/index.html)");
577:   WiFiClient client = server.client();
578:   client.flush();
579:   client.stop();
580: }
581: 
582: // Route: File Download Stream (High-throughput chunked streaming)
583: void handleDownload() {
584:   if (!server.hasArg("file")) {
585:     server.sendHeader("Connection", "close");
586:     server.send(400, "text/plain", "Missing file parameter");
587:     WiFiClient client = server.client();
588:     client.flush();
589:     client.stop();
590:     return;
591:   }
592: 
593:   String req = server.arg("file");
594:   if (!req.startsWith("/"))
595:     req = "/" + req;
596: 
597:   String resolvedPath = "";
598:   if (SD.exists(req)) {
599:     resolvedPath = req;
600:   } else if (SD.exists("/default" + req)) {
601:     resolvedPath = "/default" + req;
602:   } else if (SD.exists("/www" + req)) {
603:     resolvedPath = "/www" + req;
604:   } else if (SD.exists("/uploads" + req)) {
605:     resolvedPath = "/uploads" + req;
606:   }
607: 
608:   if (resolvedPath.length() == 0) {
609:     server.sendHeader("Connection", "close");
610:     server.send(404, "text/plain", "File Not Found on Storage");
611:     WiFiClient client = server.client();
612:     client.flush();
613:     client.stop();
614:     return;
615:   }
616: 
617:   File downloadFile = SD.open(resolvedPath, FILE_READ);
618:   if (!downloadFile || downloadFile.isDirectory()) {
619:     if (downloadFile)
620:       downloadFile.close();
621:     server.sendHeader("Connection", "close");
622:     server.send(404, "text/plain", "File Not Found on Storage");
623:     WiFiClient client = server.client();
624:     client.flush();
625:     client.stop();
626:     return;
627:   }
628: 
629:   int lastSlash = resolvedPath.lastIndexOf('/');
630:   String dlName =
631:       (lastSlash >= 0) ? resolvedPath.substring(lastSlash + 1) : resolvedPath;
632: 
633:   Serial.printf("[DOWNLOAD] Streaming: %s (%u bytes)\r\n",
634:                 resolvedPath.c_str(), (unsigned int)downloadFile.size());
635: 
636:   streamSDFile(downloadFile, "application/octet-stream", true, dlName);
637: }

639: // Helper function for reliable diagnostic requests in virtual simulation
640: static int performTestRequest(const String &url) {
641:   HTTPClient http;
642:   http.setReuse(false);
643:   http.setTimeout(8000);
644:   if (!http.begin(url)) {
645:     return -99;
646:   }
647:   int code = http.GET();
648:   // Fully drain the response stream to ensure graceful socket teardown
649:   WiFiClient *stream = http.getStreamPtr();
650:   if (stream) {
651:     uint8_t dummy[256];
652:     while (http.connected() && stream->available() > 0) {
653:       stream->read(dummy, sizeof(dummy));
654:     }
655:   }
656:   http.end();
657:   // Yield to loopTask on Core 1 to allow WebServer to complete TCP close &
658:   // rearm
659:   vTaskDelay(800 / portTICK_PERIOD_MS);
660:   return code;
661: }
662:

756:   // multi-channel scan in Wokwi)

759:   WiFi.begin(ssid, password, 6);

762:     delay(200);

764:     attempts++;

768:                     "starting Wokwi.\n",
769:                     (int)WiFi.status());
770:       WiFi.disconnect(false);
771:       WiFi.begin(ssid, password, 6);
772:     }
773:   }
774:   Serial.println("\n[NET] Wi-Fi Connected!");
775:   Serial.printf("[NET] Node IP Address: %s\n",
776:                 WiFi.localIP().toString().c_str());

786:   server.on("/get", HTTP_GET, handleDownload);

805:         client.flush();
806:         client.stop();
807:       },
